div.head: What are boreal forests?
div.p: Boreal forests are part of the largest forest region on Earth, stretching in a wide band around the northern parts of the globe. In Michigan, these forests reach the southern edge of their range, mostly along the cool, misty shorelines of the Great Lakes. The lakes play a big role in shaping the local climate by bringing cooler summers, frequent fog and mist, strong winds, heavy snowfall, and changing water levels. These conditions create a unique environment where boreal forests can thrive.

Although major wildfires and insect outbreaks are rare, they do happen occasionally and are part of the natural cycle of the forest. The trees you'll typically find here include northern white-cedar, balsam fir, white spruce, white pine, paper birch, and quaking aspen. Boreal forests also often include patches of other natural communities like rich conifer swamps, dry northern forests, and bedrock glades (

For thousands of years, Indigenous peoples have lived along the Great Lakes, using these forested shorelines for food, shelter, and cultural practices. Today, any efforts to protect and manage Michigan's boreal forests should be done in close partnership with Indigenous communities, who have deep knowledge of and long-standing relationships with these lands and waters.
What is the health of boreal forests?

Boreal forests are uncommon features of the northern Great Lakes region, occurring sporadically in the northern Lower Peninsula and infrequently in the Upper Peninsula. Analysis of General Land Office survey notes in Michigan reveals that boreal forest once occupied approximately 385,000 hectares (955,000 acres; Comer et al. 1995). Recent estimates of boreal forest in Michigan reveal a significant decrease in extent with approximations for balsam fir and white spruce forests of about 88,000 ha (215,000 ac; MIRIS 1978) and more general estimations of mixed upland conifer and other upland conifer forest of approximately 230,000 ha (575,000 ac; Michigan DNR 2001a, 2001b). Twenty-five high-quality occurrences of boreal forest, which constitute about 1,242 ha (3,000 ac) have been documented by Michigan Natural Features Inventory in Michigan's Natural Heritage Database (MNFI 2025). Turn-of-the-century logging of Northern white-cedar and other conifers from boreal forests and widespread fires following the harvests favored the conversion of mature and old-growth boreal forest to early-successional forest dominated by deciduous species (e.g., trembling aspen and paper birch; Campbell and Campbell 2000, Reich et al. 2001, Frelich 2002). Where conifer trees were eliminated or drastically reduced, hardwoods have persisted (Bergeron et al. 2004b). Many inland sites formerly dominated by boreal forest and occurring on moist to wet lacustrine soils were drained and converted to agriculture, especially in Chippewa County.

To conserve biodiversity in these systems, and when feasible, large tracts of boreal forest should remain unharvested to allow natural disturbances, such as fire when appropriate, windthrow, insect outbreaks and lake-level fluctuations, to function stochastically and generate diverse successional stages. Dead and dying wood should be retained to form snags, stumps and logs, enhancing structural complexity and habitat value (Morisette et al. 2002, Harper et al. 2005).

Helpful resources for identifying and understanding Michigan's natural communities include Michigan Natural Features Inventory's natural community classification (Cohen et al. 2015, Cohen et al. 2025) and natural community abstracts, both of which are available online along with photos, comprehensive descriptions, distribution maps, and thorough references from the scientific literature. MNFI's most detailed bibliography on Michigan's natural communities can be found in the publication "Distribution Maps of Michigan's Natural Communities" (Albert et al. 2008), which is also available for viewing and downloading at the MNFI website.

div.head: Accomplishments
div.p: Implementation of an iNaturalist project to track dwarf Lake Iris in Michigan (https://www.inaturalist.org/projects/dwarf-lake-iris-iris-lacustris-in-michigan). As of 2025, 79 people have participated, resulting in over 280 observations (Hackett et al. 2024).

With funding from USFWS and participation from State, NGO, private, and commercial entities, MNFI updated 58 existing and added 4 previously undocumented dwarf lake iris occurrences throughout Michigan from 2019-2023, which was 70% of Michigan documented occurrences (Hackett et al. 2024). Conservation easement grant awards from the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation to protect 73,000 acres in the Michigamme Highlands, which will focus on Moose habitat protection and improvement.

div.head: With funding from US
div.p: Biennial aerial survey monitoring of population in Michigan's core moose range of Iron, Baraga, and Marquette counties was conducted in 2025 and led to 171 new observations. Scientific studies featuring the Snowshoe Hare deepened understanding of conservation and silvicultural practices to manage and protect vital habitat for the species, including lowland riparian, upland spruce-fir, and young aspen habitat (Wilson et al. 2020(Wilson et al. , 2023)).

div.head: Special Concern
div.p: These medium sized moths have light wood brown forewings and contrasting dark brown spots and a sinuous dark postmedial line (Covell 1984). They occur in very wet, sedge-dominated, open to sparsely treed graminoid rich fens in the Upper Peninsula, where the larvae feed on relatively large bog buckbean plants (Johnson et al. 2017). Borers are known from 17 sites across their range, and there is a limited understanding of this species' life history traits (Natureserve 2025). The primary threats to aweme borers are habitat destruction or practices which alter system hydrology that may reduce the population size of larval hostplants. This species has been documented from five sites in five counties in Michigan as of 2025 in the state's Natural Heritage Database and four of these occurrences were observed within the last 20 years (2005-2025;MNFI 2025).

div.head: Goals
div.p: • Determine species distribution and population estimates.
• Develop host plant-and species-specific habitat management plans at all extant sites.

div.head: Special Concern
div.p: The black-backed woodpecker is a medium sized, three-toed woodpecker with a solid black back and white underparts. Adults of both sexes possess a distinct white stripe that extends from the bill to the nape and males possess a prominent and unmistakable yellow crown patch (Olson 2002, Tremblay et al. 2020). This species is restricted to the coniferous forests, swamps and bogs of the northern Lower and Upper Peninsula (Olson 2002;MNFI 2025). Though present at low densities in unburned forests with snags, this fire-dependent species is adapted to nest and forage in post-fire conditions and readily colonizes recently burned areas (Siegel et al. 2018). Breeding Bird Survey data indicate a 2.3% annual decline in Michigan between 1993 and 2019 (Sauer et al. 2020). This species has been documented from 16 sites in 11 counties in Michigan as of 2025 in the state's Natural Heritage Database and only 9 of these occurrences were observed within the last 20 years (2005-2025;MNFI 2025).

div.head: Goals
div.p: • Revisit known occurrences to determine their current status. [CPiF]
• Identify and protect unburned coniferous forests where low density populations persist.
[CPiF]
Dwarf Lake Iris

div.head: Federally and State Threatened
div.p: Dwarf lake iris is a blue-violet (rarely white), perennial flowering plant less than 6 inches tall. It reproduces primarily by cordlike, yellow-green rhizomes that are usually less than 0.2 inches thick and grow within a few inches of the ground's surface. Dwarf lake iris is endemic to the Great Lakes region, found only within a few miles of Lake Michigan and Lake Huron in Michigan and Wisconsin, USA and Ontario, CA, in boreal forest, mesic forest, fens, glades and several shoreline communities. This species has been documented from 92 sites in 11 counties in Michigan as of 2025 in the state's Natural Heritage Database and 75 of these occurrences were observed within the last 40 years (1985-2025;MNFI 2025).

div.head: Goals
div.p: • Protect and manage populations in each of the four genetically distinct groups (Cohen andTurgman-Cohen 2023, Hackett et al. 2024).
• Increase outreach efforts to developers, utilities and landowners working with populations of dwarf lake iris (Environment and Climate Canada 2023).

div.head: Lepus americanus
div.p: Snowshoe hares are medium-sized lagomorphs (3 -5 lb) that are an important prey item for many predators within boreal food webs (Burt 1948). Specifically adapted to winter landscapes, their namesake large hind feet allow efficient travel in deep snow and hares undergo coat color molts (white-to-brown in the spring and back to white in the fall) to maintain camouflage in seasonally snowy environments. Snowshoe hares may be found in a wide range of habitats but prefer sites with dense understories, which may be represented by low-lying conifers (e.g., white-cedar swamps (Thuja occidentalis)) within the boreal core of their range, but hares often use structurally similar habitats such as young aspen (Populus spp.) along southern portions of its range. Snowshoe hares reach their southern distributional limit in Michigan and this southern range boundary has shifted northwards in recent years (Burt et al. 2017). This species is not tracked in the state's Natural Heritage Database.

div.head: Goal
div.p: • Establish and maintain suitable habitat across current distribution. [PSH; IFGM]
• Better understand impacts of forest management on extant populations.

div.head: Protecting boreal forest refugia
div.p: Boreal forests in the region represent the southern edge of a cold-adapted ecosystem, supporting species that rely on persistent snow cover, cooler temperatures and high moisture levels. These forests and their associated wildlife are particularly vulnerable to changing weather impacts such as warming temperatures, increased drought and diminished snowpack. The loss of consistent winter conditions poses a significant threat to the long-term viability of boreal-dependent species. However, in the near term, lake-effect weather patterns along the north coast of Lake Michigan continue to provide cold, snowy refugia that help sustain boreal conditions. Protecting and managing these climate refuges will be essential for maintaining biodiversity and ecological function in boreal forest systems.

div.head: Focal species adaptive capacity
div.p: Adaptive capacity is a species' ability to tolerate or adapt to environmental change, whether that be through shifting in space or persisting in place (Thurman et al. 2020) Invasive & Other Problematic Species, Genes & Diseases

• Prevalence of storms and natural disturbance makes system susceptible to invasive species. More detrimental when trees/species are stressed -can respond appropriately only when healthy/functioning properly

• Population outbreaks of the native spruce budworm (Choristoneura fumiferana) and invasive balsam woolly adelgid (Adelges piceae), which feed on trees, can result in broadscale defoliation and death. While insect outbreaks are naturally cyclic, these events have been exacerbated by anthropogenic stressors (such as climate change, habitat loss, etc.)
• Where present, herbivory on rare species such as Canada yew and northern white-cedar (Thuja occidentalis), can prevent regeneration and establishment.
• Invasive species range expansion potential, such as garlic mustard (Alliaria petiolata) and glossy buckthorn (Frangula alnus).

div.head: Changing Weather Patterns
div.p: • Drought stress, changes in hydrology and flood regime, changes in wildfire frequency and severity, altered nutrient cycling and changes in invasive species, pests and pathogens (Handler et al. 2014).
• Potential for loss of species with more northerly distributions, such as calypso orchid (Calypso bulbosa) and ram's-head lady's-slipper (Cypripedium arietinum).

The historic application of cultural fires in boreal forests with red pine should be evaluated by establishing firehistories from the analysis of fire-charred stumps that remain on the landscape.

div.head: Threats and conservation actions to focal species
Lack of Knowledge
div.p: • Limited understanding of the species' life history traits (Natureserve 2025).
• Low number of known sites and limited capacity for surveying to identify new populations.

div.head: Natural Systems Modifications
div.p: • Commercial and residential development and forest activities that influence ground water levels and/or pollution.
• Destruction or removal of bog buckbean (Menyanthes trifoliata), the borer's larval hostplant.
• Limited documentation of populations and limited understanding of species' life history and biology.

div.head: Conservation Actions
div.p: Land & Water Management AWBO1. Protect large tracts of boreal forest with adjacent open peatlands to preserve ground water table. [OABM] Research & Monitoring AWBO2. Characterize aweme borer habitat in known element occurrences. AWBO3. Identify five new populations on state, federal, or privately managed lands. [OABM] Conservation Designation & Planning AWBO4. Identify management activities most beneficial to larval host plants. [OABM] Black-backed woodpecker

div.head: Threats
div.p: Natural System Modifications
• Fire suppression (Siegel et al. 2018, Tremblay et al. 2020).
• Post-fire salvage logging (Siegel et al. 2018, Tremblay et al. 2020).
• Destruction of large tracts of coniferous forest and removal of recently dead snags (Siegel et al. 2018).

div.head: Conservation Actions
div.p: Land & Water Management BBW1.

Avoid salvage logging for 5 to 8 years after a fire (Siegel 2018, Tremblay et al. 2020). Patch size of burned timber should be a minimum of 500 acres in size in large tracts or in a patchwork of large-scale disturbance.

div.head: BBW2.
div.p: Allow natural fires to burn and consider use of prescribed fire to create additional habitat (Siegel et al. 2018).

div.head: BBW3.
div.p: Protect large tracts of boreal forest and retain recently dead snags within these habitats. [LCP; LHCS]

div.head: Lack of Knowledge
div.p: • Unknown response and recovery to shoreline disturbances (e.g., canopy opening, flash flooding, sand deposition; Hackett et al. 2024) and fire.
• Unknown genetic condition, relation and exchange between Canadian and USA populations (Cohen and Turgman-Cohen 2023).

• Seed dispersal vectors, distance, limitations (Environment and Climate Change Canada 2022). [ODLI] Residential & Commercial Development • Conversion of natural forest cover to plantations, development, agriculture.
• Fire suppression may limit potential habitat.

div.p: • Population decline of near-shore populations due to increased frequency and extremity of weather events increasing flooding and substrate deposition. Research & Monitoring DLI6. Expand genetic population and adaptive analysis to include Canadian populations (Cohen and Turgman-Cohen 2023). DLI7. Monitor populations of various sizes and habitats in interoperable manner for populationand species-level trend analysis and predictions (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service 2013).
[DRP] DLI8. Understand response and recovery to sand deposition and high-water levels (Hackett et al. 2024). DLI9. Increase understanding and limitations of natural seed dispersal.

div.head: Changing Weather Patterns
div.p: • Shifts in vegetation communities over time may push habitat out of Michigan.
• Potential for increased disturbance patterns may disrupt or destroy habitat.

div.head: Conservation Actions
div.p: Land & Water Management MOOSE1. While the climate impacts to habitat are not manageable on a local scale, presence and quantity of high-quality habitat can buffer shifts in moose distribution. Make sure to protect or create high-quality moose habitat where possible.

div.head: Threats
div.p: Changing Weather Patterns

• Snowshoe Hares' coat color change is triggered by changes in day length and shortened periods of continuous snow cover in winter have resulted in longer periods of mismatch where the coat does not match the ground cover which result in increased predation and lower survival rates (Mills et al. 2013, Zimova et al. 2016, Zimova et al. 2018).

div.head: Habitat Fragmentation
div.p: • Snowshoe Hares are sensitive to habitat fragmentation and populations along southern range boundaries are often supported through immigration (Keith et al. 1993, Wirsing et al. 2002). Loss of dispersal pathways may inhibit recolonization of sites along the southern range boundary and result in permanent loss of these populations.
• Loss of habitat quality and vegetative cover impacts hare ability to hide and forage.

div.head: Conservation Actions
div.p: Land & Water Management SSH1. While the climate impacts are not manageable on a local scale, presence and quantity of high-quality habitat can buffer the negative impacts of coat-color mismatch on survival (Wilson et al. 2019). Maintaining large patches (> 5 ha) of preferred habitat can potentially slow these impacts. SSH2. Ensure protection measures for existing high-quality forested wetlands to ensure habitat connectivity. [PSH; IFGM] SSH3. Increase the prevalence of diverse conifer-dominated stands in upland regions to improve landscape heterogeneity and structural diversity. SSH4. Implement forest management practices that prioritize high stem-density conifer and deciduous stands.

div.head: Places for partnership
div.p: This map was created in collaboration with partners and highlights focal areas to work in over the next 10 years. Creating shared goals helps focus efforts and build collaboration. While this map has a select few areas highlighted, conservation work benefitting any Boreal Forest is welcome and encouraged.
How will we monitor?

div.head: Boreal Forests
div.p: • Continue to survey and update quality rankings for Boreal Forests in the state's Natural Heritage Database.
• Develop monitoring protocol for evaluating the ecological integrity of boreal forest.
• Prioritize surveys for boreal forest on private lands.

div.head: Aweme Borer
div.p: • Conduct standard black light surveys for adults.
• Monitor bog buckbean populations where aweme borer are present.
• Update element occurrences in the state's Natural Heritage Database.

div.head: Black-backed Woodpecker
div.p: • Conduct targeted surveys throughout the Upper Peninsula to document new populations • Continue annual North American Breeding Bird Survey • Use community science programs, like eBird, to assess distribution and abundance • Update element occurrences in the state's Natural Heritage Database

div.head: Dwarf Lake Iris
div.p: • Collect standardized count-based and population density measurements at least every five years.
• Document any observable changes with the area occupied for a population at least every five years.
• Update occurrences in the state's Natural Heritage Database.

div.head: Moose
div.p: • Continue standardized population surveys every two years.
• Continue Moose collar study with DNR, Keweenaw Bay Indian Community, and Northern Michigan University.

div.head: Snowshoe Hare
div.p: • Continue monitoring abundance and population trends through harvest data surveys.
